say.text: Worked case one. A 70-kg man is hit by a car. He is talking and anxious, and his skin is cold and clammy.
Pulse 120. BP 100/80. The systolic is normal, but the pulse pressure has narrowed to 20 mmHg.
Trauma shock is haemorrhagic until proven otherwise. This picture is Class II, a 15 to 30 percent loss.
Same man, a few minutes later. His systolic is still 100. Why does the pressure hold while he bleeds?

choices.label: Only 15 percent is lost, so normal systolic means a small bleed
Vasoconstriction holds systolic up until about a third of volume is lost
A normal systolic means no shock yet, so the bleed can wait
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which changes come first in a bleed: the pulse and the vessels, or the pressure?
Yes. The pulse climbs and the pulse pressure narrows first, so the systolic holds for a while.
Hypotension is the late sign. It first appears in Class III, at 31 to 40 percent loss.

choices.label: Skip the worked cases, I can read shock

say.text: That choice is not right. A normal systolic feels like proof of a small bleed, because we are taught to watch the BP.
Class I is under 15 percent loss, and this man's pulse and pulse pressure point to more. Which sign moves first?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: a normal systolic does not measure how much blood has gone.

say.text: That choice is not right. Normal numbers look like reassurance, and the eye stops at the BP.
In trauma, shock is haemorrhagic until proven otherwise, so a normal systolic does not clear him. Which sign is still worrying?

sure_note.text: You were sure: in trauma a normal number is not the end of the assessment.

say.text: Here is the full answer. The body holds the systolic by pushing the pulse up and narrowing the pulse pressure first.
Hypotension is a late sign and first appears in Class III, at 31 to 40 percent loss. A normal systolic early on is not reassurance.
The worked case gave you the reading. Now read the class yourself.
A 70-kg adult has lost about a quarter of his blood volume. Pulse is raised, BP is normal and the pulse pressure is narrowed. Which class fits, and what keeps the BP normal?

choices.label: Class I, since the pressure is normal and loss is small
Class II, but only a falling systolic would confirm it
Class II, compensated: pulse and pulse pressure move before the BP
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Match a quarter of the volume to a class, then ask which sign moves before the pressure.
Yes. Class II is a 15 to 30 percent loss, with a pulse of 100 to 120.
The pulse pressure narrows before the systolic falls, which is why the BP still reads normal.
That choice is not right. A normal pressure feels like proof the bleed is small, so Class I sounds natural.
Class I is under 15 percent loss. A quarter of the volume and a raised pulse are beyond that. What does the pulse pressure say?

sure_note.text: You were sure: a normal BP does not measure the size of the bleed.

say.text: That choice is not right. Hypotension is taught as the sign of bleeding, so a learner waits for a falling systolic before calling Class II.
The systolic does not fall until Class III. Class II is a compensated stage, so read the pulse first.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a falling systolic is a late sign, not the test for Class II.

say.text: Class II is a 15 to 30 percent loss, with a pulse of 100 to 120.
Narrowed pulse pressure comes first, and the systolic holds until about a third of volume is lost. That is why the BP reads normal here.
A 66-year-old on a beta-blocker falls from a step. Pulse 78, BP 110/70, skin pale and cool.
Which is the right reading?

choices.label: Possible shock, since a beta-blocker blunts the usual pulse rise
No shock, since pulse and BP are both normal
Minor bleed, Class I, so observe and recheck in an hour
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a beta-blocker does to the pulse before you trust a normal rate.
Yes. A beta-blocker blunts the rise in heart rate, and age limits reserve, so normal numbers can hide shock.
Pale, cool skin is the sign to act on. Children and pregnancy hide shock the same way.
That choice is not right. Normal pulse and pressure look like reassurance, so the drug and the age get skipped.
Tachycardia may be absent on beta-blockers and in the elderly, so normal numbers do not clear him. What does the skin say?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifiers: age and drugs can hide shock.

say.text: That choice is not right. A normal BP invites a small-bleed label, so Class I feels like the quick answer.
Class I is under 15 percent loss with a normal pulse. Pale, cool skin in a beta-blocked patient does not fit that label.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a normal BP does not set the class, and the skin still counts.

say.text: Beta-blockers blunt the pulse, and the elderly have less reserve, so tachycardia may be absent and normal vitals can hide shock.
Pale, cool skin is the clue. The right reading is possible shock, not a normal patient.
A man is paralysed after a fall from a roof. Which finding best separates neurogenic from haemorrhagic shock?

choices.label: Low blood pressure, since that is what bleeding causes
Poor urine output, which falls in blood loss
A slow heart rate, where bleeding would speed it up
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which finding both shock types share, then look for the one that is not shared.
Yes. Neurogenic shock from a cord injury loses sympathetic tone, so the heart rate falls, while bleeding drives it up.
Trauma shock is haemorrhagic until proven otherwise, so you rule out bleeding before you call it neurogenic.
That choice is not right. Low pressure is what bleeding causes, so it feels like the separating sign.
Both shock types can lower the pressure, so a shared finding cannot separate them. Which finding is not shared?

sure_note.text: You were sure: low BP is shared by both shocks, so it cannot be the separator.

say.text: That choice is not right. Urine output falls as blood is lost, so it feels like a reliable sign of bleeding.
Falling urine output tracks low perfusion, which both shock types share. The pulse is what separates them.

sure_note.text: You were sure: urine output does not separate neurogenic from haemorrhagic shock.

say.text: Both shock types can lower the pressure, so pressure does not separate them.
The pulse does: haemorrhage drives it up, while cord injury with loss of sympathetic tone slows it. Trauma shock is haemorrhagic until proven otherwise.
A 35-year-old has been hit in the abdomen. He is hypotensive and not responding to fluid.
What is the best first test?

choices.label: Contrast CT, since it is the most sensitive test here
Bedside FAST in the resuscitation room, with no transfer delay
CT after a stabilising trip to the scanner first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where this patient can safely be, and what the test must answer in minutes.
Yes. FAST looks for free fluid at the bedside in four windows, and imaging must not delay resuscitation.
It is the first test for intra-abdominal bleeding in an unstable patient.
That choice is not right. CT is the most accurate test for solid organs, so accuracy feels like the right first question.
The first question is whether this patient can travel. An unstable patient should not go to the CT scanner.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the most sensitive test is not automatically the first test.

say.text: That choice is not right. Stabilising first sounds careful, so the scanner feels like the next step rather than a detour.
A haemodynamically unstable patient should not be moved to the scanner. The answer is needed in the room, in minutes.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a transfer delay can kill an unstable patient.

say.text: CT is the most sensitive test, which is why it tempts. But imaging must not delay resuscitation or transfer.
FAST answers in the resuscitation room by looking for free fluid in four windows, and it is the initial bedside test for unstable bleeding.
A man with a pelvic fracture has blood at the urethral meatus and a high-riding prostate.
Before a catheter, what do you do?

choices.label: Foley catheter, to measure urine output and check
Retrograde urethrogram, to see whether the urethra is intact
Coude catheter, passed gently, to avoid trauma
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the catheter would be checking for, and which test answers that question first.
Yes. A retrograde urethrogram shows whether the urethra is intact.
A catheter is contraindicated while urethral injury is suspected, so it waits for that answer.
That choice is not right. A catheter is routine in the primary survey, so checking output feels like the first job.
Blood at the meatus and a high prostate mean the urethra may be torn. A catheter is contraindicated until it is cleared.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a routine catheter is the trap when the urethra may be torn.

say.text: That choice is not right. A gentle, angled tip feels safe, so the question seems to be technique rather than the urethra.
Technique does not settle the question. The urethra must be shown intact first.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a gentle passage does not make a torn urethra safe.

say.text: The catheter is the routine step, but blood at the meatus, perineal bruising or a high prostate forbids it until the urethra is cleared.
The retrograde urethrogram is the test that shows an intact urethra before catheterisation. Then the catheter follows.
